title: Counting the paths
objectives: Count the ways to pick $b$ from $k$ of $n$ brackets

screens.prose: Expanding $(a + b)^3$ means picking $a$ or $b$ from each bracket, then multiplying. Each path through the tree is one way to pick.
screens.question: Tap the last branch of every path that picks $b$ from exactly one bracket.

hints.text: Follow a path from the left and read off its three picks.
The path along the top picks $a$, $a$, then $b$ at the end.
The one $b$ can come from bracket 1, 2 or 3. That gives three paths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap a path only if it has one $b$ and two $a$s.

byKey.two-b: You tapped the paths with two $b$s. Those make $ab^2$. We want exactly one $b$.
byKey.a-a-a: That path picks $a$ every time, so it has no $b$ at all.
byKey.b-b-b: That path picks $b$ every time: three $b$s.
byKey.a-b-b: That path picks $b$ twice, from brackets 2 and 3.
byKey.b-a-b: That path picks $b$ twice, from brackets 1 and 3.
byKey.b-b-a: That path picks $b$ twice, from brackets 1 and 2.
byKey.a-a-b: You missed the path $a$, $a$, $b$: it takes $b$ from bracket 3 only.
byKey.a-b-a: You missed the path $a$, $b$, $a$: it takes $b$ from bracket 2 only.
byKey.b-a-a: You missed the path $b$, $a$, $a$: it takes $b$ from bracket 1 only.
byKey.a: That branch is partway along. Tap the last branch of each path, in the Bracket 3 column.
byKey.b: That branch is partway along. Tap the last branch of each path, in the Bracket 3 column.

byKey.b-b: That branch is partway along. Tap the last branch of each path, in the Bracket 3 column.

explain.text: Three paths pick one $b$: from bracket 1, 2 or 3. Each multiplies to $a^2b$, so $(a + b)^3$ has $3a^2b$. The number in front counts the paths.

screens.prose: Now $(a + b)^4$ and its $a^2b^2$ terms. Each one picks $b$ from 2 of the 4 brackets. A cell lists a first and a second bracket for $b$.

state.caption: The diagonal is out: one bracket cannot give $b$ twice

screens.question: Tap every cell that picks brackets 1 and 3 for $b$.

hints.text: Brackets 1 and 3 can be picked in either order.
Look at row 1 and at row 3.
Bracket 1 then 3 is (1, 3). Bracket 3 then 1 is (3, 1).

feedback.correct: (1, 3) and (3, 1) pick the same two brackets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the cells that use brackets 1 and 3, in either order.

byKey.r3c1: You found (1, 3). Picking bracket 3 first, then bracket 1, is in the grid too.
byKey.r1c3: You found (3, 1). Picking bracket 1 first, then bracket 3, is in the grid too.

explain.text: Brackets 1 and 3 appear twice: as (1, 3) and as (3, 1). Both give $b$ from the same two brackets, so they make the same term. Every pick of two brackets shows up twice in this grid.

screens.prose: Order does not matter: (1, 3) and (3, 1) are one pick. The number of ways to pick 2 of 4 is written $\binom{4}{2}$, read **4 choose 2**.

state.caption: Each cell is an ordered pick of two brackets

screens.question: What is $\binom{4}{2}$?

hints.text: How many cells are off the diagonal?
Each pick appears twice, like (1, 3) and (3, 1).
12 cells are off the diagonal, and each pick appears twice. So there are $12 \div 2$ picks.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells off the diagonal, then allow for each pick appearing twice.

byKey.ordered: 12 counts the cells off the diagonal. Each pick appears twice, once in each order.
byKey.all: 16 counts every cell, including the diagonal, where one bracket gives $b$ twice.
byKey.half-all: You halved all 16 cells. Take out the 4 diagonal cells first.
byKey.four: You counted the brackets. We want pairs of brackets.

explain.text: 12 cells sit off the diagonal, and each pick appears twice. So $\binom{4}{2} = \tfrac{12}{2} = 6$: the cells above the diagonal. It is the 6 in row 4 of Pascal’s triangle, in front of $a^2b^2$.

screens.prose: Now pick 3 of 5 brackets for $b$, one at a time. There are $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ ordered picks. The tree lists the orders of one pick: brackets 1, 2 and 4.
screens.question: In how many orders can brackets 1, 2 and 4 be picked?

hints.text: How many choices are there for the first pick? Then for the second?
After the first pick, two brackets are left.
3 choices, then 2, then 1: $3 \times 2 \times 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ends of the tree.

byKey.three: You counted the first picks only. Each first pick leaves 2 orders for the rest.
byKey.nine: You multiplied 3 by 3. After the first pick only 2 brackets are left, then 1.
byKey.two: You counted the orders after one first pick. There are 3 first picks.

explain.text: There are 3 choices first, then 2, then 1: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$. We write this as $3!$, read **3 factorial**. Every pick of 3 brackets turns up 6 times among the 60.

screens.prose: Each set of 3 brackets turns up $3! = 6$ times among the 60 ordered picks.
screens.question: How many ways are there to pick 3 of the 5 brackets, ignoring order? This is $\binom{5}{3}$.

hints.text: The 60 ordered picks count each set several times. How many?
Each set appears once for each of its 6 orders.
Divide the ordered picks by the orders: $60 \div 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the 60 ordered picks by the number of orders of each set.

byKey.ordered: 60 counts each set 6 times, once for each order.
byKey.third: You divided by 3. Each set has $3! = 6$ orders, not 3.
byKey.half: You divided by 2, as for pairs. A set of three has 6 orders.
byKey.product: You multiplied 5 by 3. Count the ordered picks, then divide by the orders.

explain.text: $\binom{5}{3} = \tfrac{60}{6} = 10$. Row 5 of Pascal’s triangle is 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1, and that 10 sits in front of $a^2b^3$. Counting picks finds the number without building the triangle.

screens.prose: Ten brackets: $(a + b)^{10}$. A term with $b^8$ picks $b$ from 8 brackets and $a$ from the other 2.

containers.label: Ten brackets: what each one gives

state.caption: One way to pick: $b$ from 8 brackets, $a$ from 2

screens.question: Which is larger, $\binom{10}{8}$ or $\binom{10}{2}$?

options.why: You expected more picks to mean more ways. Picking 8 for $b$ is the same as picking 2 to leave as $a$.

options.text: $\binom{10}{2}$, because 8 picks are harder to arrange
options.why: You expected the bigger pick to be rarer. Each choice of 2 for $a$ fixes the 8 for $b$.

hints.text: When you choose the 8 brackets for $b$, what else have you chosen?
The 2 brackets left over give $a$.
Choosing 8 for $b$ is the same as choosing 2 for $a$. So the counts are equal.

feedback.correct: Picking 8 for $b$ is picking 2 for $a$: 45 ways each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the brackets you leave out.

byKey.more: You expected more picks to mean more ways. Each pick of 8 for $b$ leaves exactly 2 for $a$, so the counts match.

explain.text: Each choice of 8 brackets for $b$ leaves exactly 2 for $a$, and the reverse. So $\binom{10}{8} = \binom{10}{2} = \tfrac{10 \times 9}{2} = 45$. The counts grow to the middle of the row, then shrink in the same steps.

screens.prose: Each count took the same two steps. Count the ordered picks, then divide by the $k!$ orders of each pick: $$\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}$$ The top has $k$ factors, counting down from $n$.
screens.question: What is $\binom{6}{2}$?

options.why: You stopped at $6 \times 5$. Divide by $2! = 2$ for the two orders.
You multiplied 6 by 2. The top is $6 \times 5$: two factors counting down.
You divided 6 by 2. The top is $6 \times 5$, not 6.

hints.text: How many factors go on top when $k = 2$?
The top is $6 \times 5 = 30$, and $2! = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put two factors on top, counting down from 6, then divide by $2!$.

explain.text: $\binom{6}{2} = \tfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$. Row 6 is 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1, and 15 is its third number.

screens.prose: Now write the count with factorials, where $n! = n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 1$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ ordered picks: $n$ choices, then $n - 1$, for $k$ factors
$\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$, divide by the $k!$ orders of each pick

hints.text: Which line is the count you made first, with the 60 ordered picks?
The factorial line rewrites the ordered count before anything is divided.
Ordered picks, rewrite with factorials, divide by $k!$, then check with $n = 5$ and $k = 3$.

feedback.correct: Ordered picks over the orders of each pick.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the ordered picks, and divide by $k!$ only after rewriting them.

byKey.divide: Dividing by $k!$ needs the ordered count written first.
byKey.check: The check uses the finished formula, so it comes last.

explain.text: The ordered count is $n!$ with the last $(n - k)!$ factors cancelled. Dividing by $k!$ removes the orders within each pick. So $\binom{n}{k} = \tfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$, and $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ as before.

screens.prose: A trader places 5 trades. Each wins or loses with chance 0.5, independently. So each of the $2^5 = 32$ win-loss sequences is equally likely.

state.caption: Sequences with each number of wins

screens.question: What is the chance that exactly 3 of the 5 trades win?

hints.text: How many of the 32 sequences have exactly 3 wins?
Choose which 3 of the 5 trades win.
$\binom{5}{3} = 10$ sequences, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{32}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{10}{32}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sequences with 3 wins, then divide by 32.

byKey.count: 10 is the number of sequences. Divide by the 32 equally likely sequences.
byKey.share: You took 3 out of 5. Count the win-loss sequences with 3 wins instead.
byKey.cube: You worked out $0.5^3$ for the 3 wins alone. The 2 losses and the order count too.
byKey.one-seq: That is one sequence, such as win, win, win, loss, loss. There are $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ of them.

explain.text: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ sequences have 3 wins, and each has chance $0.5^5 = \tfrac{1}{32}$. So the chance is $\tfrac{10}{32} = 0.3125$. A count of sequences times the chance of one is the binomial distribution, which comes later.

ideas: The number in front of $a^{n-k}b^k$ counts the ways to pick $b$ from $k$ of the $n$ brackets.
Count ordered picks, then divide by the $k!$ orders of each pick.
Picking $k$ brackets for $b$ is picking $n - k$ for $a$, so the counts rise and fall symmetrically.
summary.trap: More picks do not mean more ways: $\binom{10}{8} = \binom{10}{2} = 45$.

quiz.prose: A term of $(a + b)^7$ picks $b$ from 2 of the 7 brackets.
quiz.question: What is $\binom{7}{2}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered picks, then divide by $2!$.

byKey.ordered: 42 counts each pair twice, once in each order. Divide by 2.
byKey.times: You multiplied 7 by 2. The top is $7 \times 6$.
byKey.square: You picked from 7 twice, allowing the same bracket twice. The second pick has only 6 choices.

explain.text: There are $7 \times 6 = 42$ ordered picks, and each pair appears twice. So $\binom{7}{2} = 21$, the third number of row 7.

quiz.prose: In $(a + b)^6$, a term can take $b$ from any number of brackets, even none.
quiz.question: How many ways are there to pick $b$ from none of the 6 brackets?

options.why: You counted no ways. Taking $a$ from every bracket is one way: it gives the $a^6$ term.
6 counts the ways to pick exactly one bracket. Picking none can be done only one way.
720 is $6!$, the orders of all six brackets. Picking none leaves nothing to order.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about which term of $(a + b)^6$ has no $b$.

explain.text: $\binom{6}{0} = 1$: take $a$ from every bracket and get $a^6$. The formula agrees when $0! = 1$: $\tfrac{6!}{0! \, 6!} = 1$. That is why every row of Pascal’s triangle starts with 1.

quiz.prose: You want the number in front of $a^3b^9$ in $(a + b)^{12}$.
quiz.question: Which is equal to $\binom{12}{9}$?

options.why: You changed the 12 as well. The pick is still from all 12 brackets.
That is $12 \times 11 \times 10$, the ordered picks of 3. Divide by $3!$ as well.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the brackets that give $a$ instead.

explain.text: Choosing 9 brackets for $b$ leaves 3 for $a$, so $\binom{12}{9} = \binom{12}{3}$. That is $\tfrac{12 \times 11 \times 10}{6} = 220$.

quiz.prose: A fair coin is flipped 4 times.
quiz.question: What is the chance of exactly 2 heads?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sequences with 2 heads, out of all 16.

byKey.half: You took 2 heads out of 4 flips. Count the head-tail sequences with 2 heads instead.
byKey.square: You worked out $0.5^2$ for the two heads alone. The two tails and the order count too.
byKey.one-seq: That is one sequence, such as HHTT. There are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ of them.

explain.text: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ of the $2^4 = 16$ sequences have 2 heads. Each is equally likely, so the chance is $\tfrac{6}{16} = 0.375$.
